entries.test: Compare Anthropic's dated annualized revenue disclosures and their implied revenue with the revenue period and amount specified in its legal filing.
entries.note: Adding annualized snapshots does not itself establish cumulative revenue, and 'exceeding $5 billion' supplies no upper bound.

entries.test: Compare Uber's business model, revenue sources, and operating costs with those of AI companies.
entries.note: The surrounding paragraphs give 'different business' a concrete economic meaning.

entries.test: Public subscription unit economics and usage studies could establish whether unpredictable compute costs prevent monthly subscription prices from covering users' costs.
entries.note: The 'biggest mistakes' wording is evaluative, but its stated economic mechanism is testable.

entries.test: Consumer retention and purchasing data following the specified Anthropic price increases would show whether most consumers, and nearly all at $80 monthly, stop purchasing.
entries.note: The prediction depends on the specified price increase occurring.
He expresses doubt rather than a firm prediction. The immediate antecedent concerns Anthropic's proposed increases, not AI subscriptions generally.

entries.test: Public financial records showing sustained commercial viability for AI companies retaining subscriptions without directly passing through compute costs would contradict the prediction.
entries.note: In context, 'no future' means the business model cannot remain commercially viable.

entries.test: Published token-usage prediction results and documented metered-usage budgets would show whether users can anticipate consumption sufficiently to budget.
entries.note: This is an absolute practical claim, despite its emphatic wording.

entries.test: Anthropic's and OpenAI's inference revenue and attributable inference costs at publication would establish whether inference was profitable.
entries.note: 'I do not believe' introduces his substantive position; it does not assign a probability.

entries.test: Public inference cost trends, training expenditures, and documented cost-reduction options would test the claimed absence of a workable way to cut costs.
entries.note: The proposition preserves his 'appear' qualification.
He does not specify whether 'lower' and 'higher' compare with earlier periods, forecasts, or prior reporting.
The central assertion is a deliberate private intention to deceive the media.
This concerns how already-published articles would have differed under a counterfactual.
The invented dialogue conveys Zitron's own position. The scapegoat allegation attributes a private motive for the layoffs' public justification.

entries.test: Software companies' disclosed AI revenue compared with total revenue and revenue growth would establish AI's contribution.
entries.note: The surrounding company examples supply a plain reading of 'much' as a material revenue contribution.

entries.test: Compare documented AI expenditures with TARP, PPP, and other historical spending programs on a consistent accounting basis.
entries.note: Specific monetary comparisons make this checkable despite the sweeping superlative. Funding, planned capex, expenditure, and losses are distinct quantities.

entries.test: Public venture-capital returns, fundraising capacity, startup financing requirements, and intellectual-property evidence would test the claimed financing constraint and its stated causes.
entries.note: The extracted proposition principally explains an asserted inability through present financial and business conditions.

entries.test: Frontier labs' public financial results and substantiated business economics would show whether a feasible route to net profitability exists.
entries.note: This asserts present economic infeasibility, not merely current losses.
'Riddles' and 'terrible business' supply no shared standard for testing the asserted causal relationship.

entries.test: Nebius's contractual delivery requirements and installed IT capacity at publication would establish the asserted mismatch between obligations and existing infrastructure.
entries.note: He describes an existing contractual setup, rather than explicitly predicting a missed deadline. 'Set up to fail' need not imply deliberate sabotage.

entries.test: Documented completion of the full Stargate Abilene project would falsify the prediction that it never gets built.
entries.note: 'I bet' expresses a prediction here. Context concerns completion of the full project, since some buildings already exist.
'I'd be shocked' expresses low probability for early completion, not a firm exclusion.

entries.test: Debt contracts, credit analyses, and repayment structures would show whether these deals materially depend on AI demand and the borrower's continued operation.
entries.note: The stated repayment dependencies give the risk claim concrete financial content.
'AI psychosis' and 'anything ... is a natural winner' are sweeping rhetorical characterizations.

entries.test: AWS incident reports and corroborated reporting would establish whether Kiro use caused at least two recent AWS outages.
entries.note: Zitron asserts causation in his own voice while acknowledging Amazon's denial.

entries.test: Public studies measuring programming knowledge and engineering performance among people delegating all code writing to LLMs would test whether such use produces learning or improvement.
entries.note: The categorical denial of learning and improvement is empirically testable, even though 'developing code' has definitional ambiguity.

entries.test: Documented engineering workflows and evaluations of coding tools would show whether they perform engineering responsibilities or leave correctness judgments to users while producing flattering feedback.
entries.note: The surrounding discussion gives the claim a practical meaning centered on responsibility for understanding and validating code.

entries.test: Public evaluations of wholly LLM-generated codebases would test whether complete code generation guarantees functional quality, comprehensibility, or useful results.
entries.note: In context, 'all code' means all the code for a project, not every conceivable program. The caveat denies a guarantee rather than asserting that generated code is always bad.
